messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 55-year-old African American bomb disposal technician married to his high school sweetheart, was profoundly affected by the natural disaster that occurred six months ago. The event, a devastating tornado, not only swept through his neighborhood but also triggered memories of his military service and bomb disposal operations. On the day of the tornado, John was at home when he heard a sudden loud roar outside. He immediately recognized it as something dangerous. As he rushed to secure his family, the unpredictable nature of the event left him in constant fear for their lives. The moment the sirens began to wail and shouting could be heard from neighbors, his body reacted before he had time to think. He found himself diving into a safe room, his heart racing as if he were back in combat. Since then, John has been plagued by unpredictable situations that trigger intense flashbacks and false alarms. Any loud noise or sudden shout can send him spiraling into panic, reliving the chaos of the tornado. This unpredictability exacerbates his sense of danger; his body reacts as though he is still under threat even when there’s no real peril. To cope with this distress, John often turns to maladaptive strategies. He eats excessively to numb his emotions and avoids anything that could be stressful. His need for mental distraction keeps him constantly occupied, often working late into the night on trivial tasks. However, these behaviors only serve to heighten his triggers. The more he isolates himself or distracts himself with food and work, the more he remains hyper-vigilant to any sudden noise or unpredictable event. John’s memory of the tornado is fragmented and incomplete. He finds himself pushing away the full recall before it can settle, leaving him with only bits and pieces that feel like a puzzle without an answer. When he does manage to remember parts of what happened, intense rage surges through him, fueling his false alarms and making him react as though danger is imminent. The cycle tightens further when John recalls the event, igniting both his sense of threat and his triggers. The fragmented memories and intense emotions trigger more frequent false alarms and flashbacks, leading to a heightened state of arousal that only exacerbates his maladaptive coping mechanisms. He often overeats or avoids social gatherings, pushing himself deeper into isolation. Despite these efforts to manage his distress, John’s life has become increasingly difficult. His work as a bomb disposal technician requires him to be in unpredictable and potentially dangerous situations daily. The unpredictability of his job now triggers intense reactions that interfere with his ability to perform tasks safely and effectively. His wife notices the changes too; he is often distant and irritable, struggling to connect emotionally. What finally brought John to seek help was a near-miss incident at work where his heightened state of arousal led him to misjudge a situation critically. He realized that if he didn’t get help soon, he would either lose his job or worse, put himself and others in grave danger. John is most afraid of losing control again—of being unable to predict when the next false alarm will strike and how it might affect those around him. Yet, he hopes for a way to regain a sense of calm and stability, to be able to face unpredictable situations without feeling like his body is reacting out of control. He dreams of a day when he can return to work without fear, and more importantly, connect with his family in a meaningful way again.
